Intraaortic balloon pump therapy alters the arterial pressure waveform — pulse contour analysis is inaccurate and contraindicated.
Dysrhythmias (atrial fibrillation, SVT) cause beat-to-beat variation that makes pulse contour analysis unreliable — contraindicated.
A mechanically ventilated patient in sinus rhythm post-bowel repair is the ideal candidate — SVV and PPV accurately predict fluid responsiveness in this setting.

stem: A patient has a noninvasive cuff BP of 70/40 mm Hg but the intraarterial catheter in the same arm reads 108/70 mm Hg. What is the best action?
opts: Place the patient in Trendelenburg position
Assess the cuff for proper arm size
rat: A discrepancy of 10-20 mm Hg between invasive and noninvasive BP is expected — invasive is normally higher. A difference this large (>30 mm Hg) often indicates an incorrectly sized BP cuff. The invasive line is more reliable. Before initiating clinical interventions like rapid response or fluid bolus, troubleshoot the noninvasive measurement first.
optRationales: The arterial line reads 108/70 which is normal — activating rapid response based solely on an inaccurate cuff reading would be inappropriate.
Trendelenburg positioning is used for hypotension — the invasive reading of 108/70 does not indicate true hypotension.
An oversized or undersized BP cuff can falsely lower or raise readings — assessing cuff size is the appropriate first troubleshooting step.
A fluid bolus for hypotension is not indicated when the invasive reading (more reliable) shows 108/70 — treat the patient, not the monitor.

stem: A patient with congestive heart failure becomes anxious and tachypneic when placed supine for a PAOP measurement. What is the best action?
opts: Limit supine position to no more than 10 seconds
Administer anxiety medication while recording the pressure
Encourage slow deep breaths while supine
Elevate the head of bed to 45° while recording pressures
rat: Hemodynamic parameters can be accurately measured and trended with HOB up to 45° as long as the transducer is leveled to the phlebostatic axis. For a patient who is intolerant of the supine position (especially with CHF), HOB 45° is the optimal compromise. Anxiety medications and slow breathing can alter hemodynamic readings.
optRationales: Limiting supine time to 10 seconds is not sufficient to obtain accurate readings and does not address the patient's distress.
Anxiety medications are not standard care for hemodynamic measurement — they would alter the patient's hemodynamic state.
Encouraging deep breaths while supine alters intrathoracic pressure, which would make PAOP readings inaccurate.
HOB at 45° with the transducer leveled to the phlebostatic axis provides accurate readings while preventing respiratory distress in this CHF patient.

stem: A patient returns from the cardiac catheterization lab following PAC insertion and is transferred to bed. Prior to obtaining a cardiac output, what is the most important action?
opts: Zero reference the transducer at the phlebostatic axis
Inflate the PAC balloon with 1 mL air
Inject 10 mL 0.9% NS into the proximal port
rat: After any patient movement, the transducer position changes relative to the phlebostatic axis. Zero referencing must be performed before any hemodynamic measurements to ensure accuracy. Without this step, all values — including the cardiac output — will be inaccurate.
optRationales: A PAOP should be documented before CO, but zero referencing must come first to ensure the PAOP itself is accurate after the patient was moved.
Zero referencing after patient movement re-establishes the accurate baseline for all hemodynamic measurements — this must occur before any readings.
Inflating the balloon is appropriate before obtaining PAOP, but not required before obtaining thermodilution cardiac output.
10 mL of saline into the proximal port is the injectate for thermodilution CO — but zero referencing must be confirmed first to ensure accuracy.

stem: The charge nurse is supervising four critical care patients with invasive hemodynamic monitoring. Which patient should be evaluated first?
opts: A patient in cardiogenic shock with CO of 2.0 L/min
A patient with pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 20 mm Hg
A hypovolemic patient with CVP of 6 mm Hg
A patient with PAOP of 10 mm Hg
rat: CO of 2.0 L/min (normal 4-8) in a patient with cardiogenic shock is critically low — immediate assessment and intervention needed. PAP 20 mm Hg, CVP 6 mm Hg, and PAOP 10 mm Hg are all within normal limits.
optRationales: CO of 2.0 L/min in cardiogenic shock is critically below normal (4-8 L/min) — immediate assessment is required.
PAP systolic of 20 mm Hg is within normal range (15-25 mm Hg) — no immediate action required.
CVP of 6 mm Hg is within normal range (2-8 mm Hg) in a hypovolemic patient being managed — no immediate action required.
PAOP of 10 mm Hg is within normal range (8-12 mm Hg) — no immediate action required.

stem: A mechanically ventilated patient with a radial arterial line shows a 20 mm Hg decrease in arterial BP during the inspiratory phase of ventilation. What is the best interpretation?
opts: The patient may require fluid resuscitation
The arterial line may need to be replaced
The left limb may have reduced perfusion
rat: Systolic blood pressure variation (SPV) or decrease >10 mm Hg during positive pressure ventilation indicates fluid responsiveness — the patient's cardiac output is preload-dependent. Positive pressure inspiration increases intrathoracic pressure, reducing venous return and systolic BP. This is a predictor of fluid responsiveness.
optRationales: BP variation with the respiratory cycle is a known hemodynamic phenomenon — it does not indicate ventilator malfunction.
SPV >10 mm Hg in a ventilated patient indicates preload dependence and fluid responsiveness — fluid resuscitation would likely improve cardiac output.
SPV is a clinical finding indicating fluid responsiveness — it does not indicate arterial line malfunction.
The finding reflects systemic hemodynamics related to intrathoracic pressure — not limb-specific perfusion.

stem: The nurse notices a slightly dampened arterial waveform and blood backed up into the pressure tubing. What is the best action?
opts: Check the inflation volume of the flush system pressure bag
Disconnect the flush system from the arterial line catheter
Zero reference the transducer at the phlebostatic axis
Reduce the number of stopcocks in the flush system tubing
rat: Blood backing up into pressure tubing indicates the flush bag pressure has fallen below 300 mm Hg — the minimum pressure needed to maintain a continuous 3 mL/hr forward flush. The pressure bag must be inflated to 300 mm Hg to prevent backward blood flow. Disconnecting increases infection risk. Zero referencing corrects leveling errors, not flow issues.
optRationales: Blood backing up into pressure tubing means the flush bag is under-pressurized — inflating it to 300 mm Hg restores forward flow and clears the blood.
Disconnecting the flush system from the arterial line risks infection and is never an appropriate action for this problem.
Zero referencing corrects transducer leveling errors and affects reading accuracy — it does not address blood backing up from insufficient flush pressure.
Reducing stopcocks helps prevent disconnection risk — it does not address the immediate issue of insufficient flush bag pressure.

stem: A patient has a left radial arterial line and a right subclavian pulmonary artery catheter. Which action best ensures patient safety with invasive hemodynamic monitoring lines?
opts: Ensure alarm limits are turned on
rat: Activated alarm limits are the highest safety priority in hemodynamic monitoring — alarms alert the nurse to life-threatening changes in hemodynamics, dysrhythmias, or line disconnection. Documentation, tubing length, and zero referencing are all important but secondary to active alarm surveillance.
optRationales: Documenting waveform values is important for trending — but it does not provide real-time safety alerts.
Limiting tubing length reduces waveform dampening and improves accuracy — but does not provide patient safety alerts.
Zero referencing ensures accuracy — but it is performed per policy, not daily, and does not provide active safety monitoring.
Alarm limits alert the nurse to critical changes in hemodynamic values or line disconnection in real time — the highest safety priority.

stem: The nurse is preparing to measure thermodilution cardiac output (TdCO) via a PAC. Which action best ensures patient safety?
opts: Ensure the transducer is zero referenced at the phlebostatic axis
Avoid infusing vasoactive agents in the port used to obtain TdCO
Maintain 300 mm Hg on the flush solution pressure bag
Limit pressure tubing length to a maximum of 48 inches
rat: During TdCO measurement, 10 mL of injectate is rapidly infused through the proximal port. If vasoactive agents (vasopressors, inotropes) are infusing in that same port, they will be delivered as a rapid bolus — potentially causing dangerous hemodynamic changes. The other actions ensure accuracy but do not address safety specifically.
optRationales: Zero referencing ensures accurate readings — it is an accuracy measure but not the primary safety concern for TdCO.
Rapidly injecting 10 mL of saline for TdCO will bolus any vasoactive drug co-infusing in that port — potentially causing dangerous arrhythmias or hemodynamic changes.
300 mm Hg on the flush bag ensures patency — an accuracy and maintenance measure, not specific to TdCO safety.
Limiting tubing length reduces signal dampening — an accuracy measure, not the primary safety concern for TdCO.

stem: When performing an initial pulmonary artery occlusion pressure (PAOP), which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
opts: Inflate the balloon for no more than 8 to 10 seconds while noting the waveform change
Inflate the balloon with air, recording the volume necessary to obtain a reading
Maintain the balloon in the inflated position for 8 hours following insertion
Zero reference and level the transducer air-fluid interface at the phlebostatic axis
Inflate and deflate the balloon on an hourly schedule
rat: To obtain an accurate PAOP: (1) balloon is inflated for ≤8-10 seconds until the waveform changes from PA waveform to PAOP waveform, (2) document the volume of air used, and (3) zero reference and level at the phlebostatic axis. Keeping the balloon inflated causes pulmonary infarction. Routine inflation/deflation on schedule has no indication.
optRationales: Balloon inflation ≤8-10 seconds prevents pulmonary infarction while allowing PAOP waveform to be identified — correct.
Recording the balloon inflation volume is important documentation and helps detect if the balloon requires less air over time (suggesting distal migration) — correct.
Maintaining balloon inflation causes pulmonary infarction by obstructing pulmonary blood flow — never appropriate after PAOP is obtained.
Zero referencing and leveling at the phlebostatic axis ensures accurate readings before obtaining PAOP — correct.
Routine scheduled inflation and deflation has no clinical indication — the balloon is only inflated when obtaining PAOP readings.

stem: The nurse is preparing to obtain a right atrial pressure (RAP/CVP) reading. Which nursing actions are most appropriate? Select all that apply.
opts: Compare measured pressures with other physiological parameters
Flush the central venous catheter with 20 mL of sterile saline before measurement
Inflate the balloon with 3 mL air and record the pressure tracing
Obtain the reading during end exhalation
Zero reference the transducer at the level of the phlebostatic axis
rat: For accurate RAP/CVP: zero reference at phlebostatic axis, measure at end exhalation (when intrathoracic pressure effects are minimized), and correlate with clinical assessment. Flushing before measurement is not required — the continuous saline flush maintains patency. There is no balloon on a CVP catheter — balloon inflation is specific to the PAC.
optRationales: Comparing measured pressure with clinical assessment ensures the value is accurate and clinically meaningful — correct.
Flushing with 20 mL saline before measurement is unnecessary — the continuous saline flush system maintains catheter patency.
There is no balloon on a CVP/RAP catheter — balloons are only on pulmonary artery catheters.
End exhalation minimizes the effect of respiratory variation on RAP readings in spontaneously breathing patients — correct.
Zero referencing at the phlebostatic axis ensures the transducer is properly calibrated for accurate readings — correct.

stem: During insertion of a pulmonary artery catheter, which are priority nursing actions? Select all that apply.
opts: Obtain informed consent by informing the patient of procedural risks
Allay the patient's anxiety by providing information about the procedure
Ensure that a sterile field is maintained throughout the insertion procedure
Inflate the balloon during the procedure when indicated by the physician
Monitor the patient's cardiac rhythm throughout the entire procedure
rat: During PAC insertion the nurse: reduces patient anxiety, maintains sterile field to prevent infection, inflates the balloon on physician request to assist flotation, and monitors cardiac rhythm (VT/VF can occur as the catheter passes through the right ventricle). Informed consent is obtained by the physician before the procedure — the nurse may witness it but not obtain it.
optRationales: Informed consent is the physician's responsibility and must be completed before the procedure begins — the nurse witnesses but does not obtain it.
Providing information reduces patient anxiety and promotes cooperation — an important nursing role during procedures.
Maintaining sterile technique prevents catheter-related bloodstream infection — a critical nursing responsibility.
The nurse inflates the balloon when requested to assist in floating the catheter through the right heart to the pulmonary artery.
The right ventricle is highly irritable during PAC passage — continuous cardiac monitoring is essential to detect and respond to dysrhythmias.

stem: Which nursing actions are most important for a patient with a right radial arterial line? Select all that apply.
opts: Restraining all four extremities with soft limb restraints
Checking circulation to the right hand every 2 hours
Ensuring all tubing junctions are tightly connected
Maintaining a pressurized flush solution at 300 mm Hg
Monitoring the waveform on the monitor for dampening
rat: Arterial line care: assess distal circulation q2h (ischemia risk), maintain 300 mm Hg flush pressure (prevents blood backup), and monitor for waveform dampening (indicates clot, air, or pressure issue). Ensuring tight connections prevents hemorrhage. Restraining all four extremities is never appropriate — only the involved extremity may need gentle restraint based on patient condition.
optRationales: Neurovascular checks every 2 hours detect arterial occlusion or thrombosis causing limb ischemia — essential safety monitoring.
300 mm Hg pressure maintains continuous 3 mL/hr forward flush, preventing blood backup and clot formation in the system.
Waveform dampening indicates partial occlusion, air bubbles, or kinked tubing — early detection allows prompt correction.
Restraining all four extremities is not appropriate — only the hand with the arterial line may need gentle restraint if the patient is confused.
Tight connections prevent disconnection — important but the rationale states A, B, C are the most important (E is correct but was excluded from the answer in the source).

stem: Which conditions may result in a low cardiac output and low cardiac index? Select all that apply.
rat: Low CO/CI results from reduced preload (hypovolemia), reduced contractility (MI, cardiomyopathy), increased afterload, or severe vasodilation (shock). Exercise and fever both increase metabolic demand and stimulate sympathetic activity — they typically increase cardiac output.
optRationales: Exercise increases sympathetic tone and metabolic demand — cardiac output increases during exercise, not decreases.
Hypovolemia reduces preload (venous return) — decreased filling reduces stroke volume and cardiac output.
Myocardial infarction destroys contractile myocardium — reduced contractility directly decreases cardiac output.
Shock (cardiogenic, obstructive, or distributive with myocardial dysfunction) impairs cardiac output through multiple mechanisms.
Fever increases metabolic rate and sympathetic activation — cardiac output typically increases with fever as a compensatory response.

stem: A post-CABG patient arrives in the ICU on mechanical ventilation. ABGs: pH 7.31, PaCO2 48, HCO3 22, PaO2 115, SpO2 99%. How should the nurse interpret these values?
opts: Normal ABG with high oxygen level
Partly compensated respiratory acidosis, normal oxygenation
Uncompensated metabolic acidosis with high oxygen
rat: pH 7.31 = acidosis. PaCO2 48 = elevated (respiratory cause). HCO3 22 = normal (no metabolic compensation). Uncompensated respiratory acidosis. PaO2 115 is above normal (80-100) = hyperoxygenation.
optRationales: pH 7.31 is below normal (7.35-7.45) — this is not a normal ABG.
Partly compensated would show HCO3 rising above 26 mEq/L — HCO3 is normal at 22, so no compensation has occurred.
Metabolic acidosis would show low HCO3 — HCO3 is normal, and the primary driver is elevated PaCO2 (respiratory).
pH 7.31 = acidosis, elevated PaCO2 = respiratory cause, normal HCO3 = no compensation, PaO2 115 = hyperoxygenation. Correct interpretation.

stem: A patient on assist/control ventilation (TV 600 mL, RR 14) is spontaneously breathing at 22 breaths/min. What ABG abnormality is most likely to develop?
rat: In assist/control mode, every patient-initiated breath — even spontaneous ones — triggers a full preset tidal volume. With 22 spontaneous breaths/min each delivering 600 mL, excessive CO2 is blown off, leading to respiratory alkalosis.
optRationales: Metabolic acidosis results from non-respiratory causes (lactic acidosis, DKA, etc.) — not from over-ventilation.
Metabolic alkalosis results from HCO3 excess or H+ loss (vomiting, diuretics) — not from mechanical ventilation patterns.
Respiratory acidosis requires hypoventilation and CO2 retention — this patient is over-ventilating.
Assist/control delivers full TV with every triggered breath — 22 breaths/min × 600 mL causes CO2 washout and respiratory alkalosis.

stem: After increasing PEEP from 10 to 15 cm H2O and FiO2 from 0.60 to 0.70, the patient's BP drops from 120/76 to 90/60 mm Hg. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Decreased cardiac output from increased intrathoracic pressure
rat: High PEEP increases intrathoracic pressure, which impedes venous return to the right heart. Reduced preload decreases cardiac output, reflected as hypotension. This is the most common hemodynamic complication of high PEEP.
optRationales: Higher PEEP increases intrathoracic pressure → impedes venous return → decreased preload → decreased cardiac output → hypotension. This is the mechanism.
Hypovolemia could cause hypotension, but there is no indication of volume loss — the timing directly follows the PEEP increase.
Higher PEEP decreases — not increases — venous return by raising intrathoracic pressure.
Oxygen toxicity damages alveoli over time — it does not cause acute hemodynamic changes like immediate hypotension.

stem: Regarding endotracheal suctioning, which statement is most accurate?
opts: It is performed based on patient assessment findings
Saline instillation should precede suctioning to loosen secretions
rat: Suctioning is an as-needed intervention based on clinical assessment — not done on a routine schedule. It is associated with ICP increases (not decreases), can stimulate the cough reflex, and saline instillation is not recommended as it does not loosen secretions and has negative physiological effects.
optRationales: Suctioning increases intracranial pressure — hyperoxygenation before suctioning helps mitigate this risk.
Suctioning can stimulate the cough reflex — it does not depress it.
Suctioning is performed when assessment findings indicate need (secretions, decreased SpO2, audible secretions) — not on a fixed schedule.
Saline instillation is not recommended — it does not loosen secretions and is associated with negative outcomes including SpO2 drops and infection risk.

stem: A patient with COPD and pneumonia has ABGs on room air: pH 7.35, PaCO2 55, HCO3 30, PaO2 65. How should the nurse interpret these values?
opts: Normal oxygenation and partly compensated metabolic alkalosis
Normal oxygenation and uncompensated respiratory acidosis
rat: PaO2 65 < 80 = hypoxemia. PaCO2 55 = elevated = respiratory acidosis. HCO3 30 = elevated = metabolic compensation. pH 7.35 = normal = fully compensated. This COPD patient has a chronic compensated respiratory acidosis with acute hypoxemia.
optRationales: Metabolic alkalosis would show the primary problem as HCO3 elevation — here the primary problem is elevated PaCO2 (respiratory acidosis) with HCO3 elevated as compensation.
PaO2 65 = hypoxemia, PaCO2 55 = respiratory acidosis, HCO3 30 = elevated compensation, pH 7.35 = normal = fully compensated respiratory acidosis. Correct.
PaO2 65 is below the normal range of 80-100 mm Hg — this is hypoxemia.
The elevated HCO3 (30) indicates metabolic compensation has occurred — this is not uncompensated.

stem: A pulmonologist wants a patient to receive 10 ventilator breaths/min but also breathe spontaneously between those breaths at their own tidal volume. Which ventilation mode is being described?
rat: SIMV delivers a preset rate and tidal volume but allows the patient to breathe spontaneously between machine breaths at their own tidal volume. A/C delivers the full preset TV with every triggered breath. Controlled ventilation does not allow spontaneous breathing. PEEP is an adjunct, not a standalone mode.
optRationales: Assist/control delivers the full preset tidal volume with every triggered breath — spontaneous breaths get the same TV as mandatory breaths, not their own.
Controlled ventilation delivers breaths at a set rate with no patient triggering — spontaneous efforts cause dyssynchrony.
SIMV delivers mandatory breaths at a set rate while allowing spontaneous breaths at the patient's own tidal volume between them — the mode described.
PEEP adds positive pressure at end-expiration — it is an adjunct applied to other modes, not a standalone ventilation mode.

stem: After retaping an endotracheal tube, the nurse auscultates absent breath sounds over the left lung. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The ETT advanced into the right mainstem bronchus
The patient has a left pneumothorax
The patient aspirated secretions during the procedure
rat: ETT repositioning can inadvertently advance the tube into the right mainstem bronchus (the more vertical of the two). This causes right lung ventilation only, with absent sounds on the left. This must be corrected immediately by withdrawing the tube to the appropriate position.
optRationales: ETT repositioning can advance the tube into the right mainstem bronchus — aeration of only the right lung causes absent sounds on the left. Most likely cause.
Pneumothorax would also cause absent sounds but is not associated with ETT repositioning — the clinical context points to tube displacement.
Aspiration may occur during procedures but presents with radiographic changes and hypoxemia — not immediate unilateral absent breath sounds.
Stethoscope malfunction is always possible but not the most clinically relevant or likely cause in this context.

stem: A mode of pressure-targeted ventilation that augments spontaneous breaths by delivering a preset amount of inspiratory positive pressure through the ETT is called:
rat: Pressure support augments each spontaneous breath with a preset inspiratory pressure to reduce the work of breathing. CPAP applies positive pressure throughout the respiratory cycle for spontaneous breaths. PEEP applies positive pressure at end-expiration during mechanical breaths. T-piece provides unassisted oxygen delivery.
optRationales: CPAP applies continuous positive pressure throughout the respiratory cycle — it does not provide inspiratory augmentation per breath.
PEEP applies positive pressure at end-expiration — it does not augment inspiratory effort.
Pressure support delivers a preset inspiratory pressure boost with each spontaneous breath through the ETT — reduces work of breathing.
A T-piece provides supplemental oxygen for spontaneous unassisted breaths — there is no pressure support.

stem: While neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs) are used in some ventilated patients, what is their primary mechanism of action?
rat: NMBAs block neuromuscular transmission at the motor end plate, causing skeletal muscle paralysis including the respiratory muscles. They have no sedative, analgesic, or anticonvulsant properties — sedation and analgesia must always be provided separately when NMBAs are used.
optRationales: NMBAs have no analgesic properties — pain management must be provided separately and is critical since the patient cannot communicate distress.
NMBAs have no anticonvulsant effect — seizure activity may continue undetected under paralysis.
NMBAs block neuromuscular transmission causing complete skeletal muscle paralysis — their sole mechanism of action.
NMBAs have no sedative properties — sedation must always be administered concurrently to prevent awareness during paralysis.

stem: What is the earliest sign of hypoxemia's effect on the nervous system?
rat: The brain is highly sensitive to oxygen deprivation. Restlessness and agitation are the earliest CNS signs of hypoxemia. Cyanosis is a late sign requiring significant desaturation. Tachycardia is an early cardiovascular sign. Tachypnea is an early respiratory compensatory sign — but CNS changes typically precede these.
optRationales: Cyanosis requires approximately 5 g/dL of deoxygenated hemoglobin — it is a late sign of severe hypoxemia.
Restlessness and agitation are the earliest CNS manifestations of hypoxemia — the brain responds quickly to decreased oxygen delivery.
Tachycardia is an early cardiovascular compensatory response to hypoxemia — but neurological changes (restlessness) typically appear first.
Tachypnea is an early respiratory compensatory sign — but CNS changes tend to precede it.

stem: The amount of effort needed to maintain a given level of ventilation is referred to as:
rat: Work of breathing (WOB) is the effort required to maintain ventilation. Compliance is the distensibility/stretchability of the lungs and chest wall. Resistance is opposition to gas flow in the airways. Tidal volume is the volume of a typical breath.
optRationales: Compliance measures how easily the lungs and chest wall stretch — decreased compliance (stiff lungs) increases work of breathing.
Resistance refers to opposition to airflow in the airways — increased resistance (bronchospasm) also increases work of breathing.
Tidal volume is the volume of air in a single breath — it is a parameter, not a measure of effort.
Work of breathing is specifically defined as the effort required to maintain a given level of ventilation.

stem: Which oxygen delivery device is best suited to deliver 65% FiO2 to a spontaneously breathing patient?
rat: Non-rebreathing reservoir masks deliver 60-80% FiO2 depending on flow rate, fit, and breathing pattern — appropriate for delivering 65%. Nasal cannula delivers 24-44% FiO2. Simple face mask delivers up to 60%. Venturi masks are precise but typically limited to ≤60%.
optRationales: Non-rebreathing reservoir masks deliver 60-80% FiO2 — the reservoir stores high-concentration oxygen for delivery during inspiration. Best choice for 65%.
Low-flow nasal cannula delivers only 24-44% FiO2 (1-6 L/min) — far below the 65% needed.
Simple face mask delivers 35-60% FiO2 — cannot reliably achieve 65%.
Venturi masks deliver precise low-to-moderate FiO2 (24-60%) — better for COPD patients needing controlled O2, not high concentrations.

stem: A patient on SIMV (RR 4/min) with spontaneous rate of 12/min receives morphine. Respiratory rate drops to 4/min. Which acid-base disturbance is most likely?
rat: Morphine causes respiratory depression. The patient was relying on 12 spontaneous breaths/min for most of their ventilation. With rate now only 4/min (all from the ventilator), alveolar ventilation is greatly reduced, CO2 accumulates, and respiratory acidosis develops.
optRationales: Metabolic acidosis results from non-respiratory H+ gain or HCO3 loss — this is a purely respiratory problem from opioid-induced hypoventilation.
Metabolic alkalosis results from HCO3 excess — not from respiratory depression.
Morphine-induced respiratory depression reduces alveolar ventilation → CO2 retention → respiratory acidosis.
Respiratory alkalosis results from hyperventilation and CO2 washout — this patient is hypoventilating.

stem: After morphine causes respiratory depression in a SIMV patient (rate drops from 12 to 4/min), what ventilator adjustment is most appropriate?
opts: Change to assist/control at rate of 4/min
rat: The patient has lost their spontaneous breathing contribution. Increasing the SIMV rate provides more mandatory breaths to compensate for the lost spontaneous ventilation and prevents CO2 retention. Naloxone should also be considered to reverse the morphine.
optRationales: PEEP improves oxygenation by increasing end-expiratory lung volume — it does not increase ventilation rate or correct hypoventilation.
Pressure support augments spontaneous breaths — but the patient now has minimal spontaneous effort, making PSV ineffective.
Changing to A/C at rate of 4/min does not solve the problem — the rate is still too low for adequate ventilation.
Increasing the SIMV mandatory rate compensates for the patient's lost spontaneous breathing and restores adequate minute ventilation.

stem: What is the primary risk rationale for preferring endotracheal over nasotracheal intubation?
rat: Nasotracheal tubes pass through the nasal passages and sinuses, significantly increasing the risk for sinusitis, which can seed ventilator-associated pneumonia. This infection risk is the primary reason orotracheal intubation is preferred.
optRationales: Basilar skull fracture is a contraindication to nasal intubation — but it is a contraindication, not the primary reason for preference of oral route in general.
Nasotracheal intubation can be performed without cervical hyperextension — it is sometimes preferred for cervical spine injuries.
Patients with nasotracheal tubes are generally more comfortable and better able to mouth words — this is actually an advantage of the nasal route.
Nasotracheal tubes increase risk for sinusitis, which can progress to ventilator-associated infection — this is the primary clinical reason orotracheal intubation is preferred.

stem: Oxygen saturation (SaO2) specifically represents:
rat: SaO2 reflects the percentage of hemoglobin binding sites occupied by oxygen. Alveolar oxygen tension is PAO2. Dissolved plasma oxygen is represented by PaO2. Total oxygen consumption is VO2.
optRationales: Alveolar oxygen tension is PAO2 — calculated from the alveolar gas equation, not measured by SaO2.
SaO2 is the percentage of hemoglobin that is saturated (chemically combined) with oxygen — the definition of oxygen saturation.
Oxygen dissolved in plasma is represented by PaO2 — it accounts for only a small fraction of total oxygen content.
Total oxygen consumption (VO2) is calculated from the Fick equation — not measured by SaO2 alone.

stem: What does pulse oximetry (SpO2) measure?
rat: Pulse oximetry uses light absorption to estimate oxygen saturation of hemoglobin in peripheral tissues. It does not measure ABGs, hemoglobin levels, or oxygen consumption — those require blood sampling or additional equipment.
optRationales: ABGs require an arterial blood sample — pulse oximetry provides a non-invasive estimate of SaO2 but not pH, PaCO2, or exact PaO2.
Hemoglobin concentration requires a blood count — pulse oximetry measures saturation, not the amount of hemoglobin.
Oxygen consumption (VO2) requires both arterial and mixed venous sampling via pulmonary artery catheter — not measured by SpO2.
Pulse oximetry uses light wavelengths to measure the saturation of hemoglobin with oxygen in peripheral capillaries.

stem: A PaCO2 of 48 mm Hg is associated with which condition?
rat: Normal PaCO2 is 35-45 mm Hg. A value of 48 indicates CO2 retention from hypoventilation — inadequate alveolar ventilation allows CO2 to accumulate. Hyperventilation lowers PaCO2. PaCO2 does not directly affect O2 absorption. Increased HCO3 excretion would cause metabolic acidosis.
optRationales: Hyperventilation blows off CO2 — it decreases PaCO2 below 35 mm Hg.
Hypoventilation results in CO2 retention — PaCO2 rises above 45 mm Hg. A value of 48 reflects hypoventilation.
PaCO2 does not directly affect oxygen absorption — that is influenced by PaO2 and hemoglobin.
Increased HCO3 excretion by the kidneys would lower serum HCO3, causing metabolic acidosis — unrelated to PaCO2.

stem: A non-intubated patient with hypoxemia on ABG has a respiratory rate of 22/min. What is the nurse's first intervention?
rat: Supplemental oxygen is the first-line treatment for hypoxemia. Escalation to BiPAP or intubation is considered only if oxygen therapy fails to correct hypoxemia. Oropharyngeal suctioning is not indicated without evidence of secretion obstruction.
optRationales: Emergency intubation is not warranted as a first response to hypoxemia in a spontaneously breathing patient — oxygen therapy comes first.
BiPAP is a step-up intervention considered if supplemental oxygen alone does not adequately correct hypoxemia.
Supplemental oxygen is always the first intervention for hypoxemia — simple, immediate, and effective as first-line treatment.
Suctioning the oropharynx is indicated for secretion management — there is no indication of secretions in this scenario.

stem: A patient presents with agitation, finger numbness and tingling. ABGs: pH 7.51, PaCO2 25, HCO3 25. How should the nurse interpret these values?
rat: pH 7.51 = alkalosis. PaCO2 25 = low = respiratory cause (hyperventilation). HCO3 25 = normal = no metabolic compensation. Uncompensated respiratory alkalosis. Numbness/tingling and agitation are classic symptoms of hyperventilation-induced alkalosis.
optRationales: Compensated metabolic alkalosis would show elevated HCO3 as the primary problem with high PaCO2 as compensation — HCO3 is normal here.
Normal ABG values are pH 7.35-7.45, PaCO2 35-45, HCO3 22-26 — pH 7.51 and PaCO2 25 are both abnormal.
Respiratory acidosis requires elevated PaCO2 and low pH — PaCO2 is low (25) and pH is elevated here.
Low PaCO2 (hyperventilation), high pH (alkalosis), normal HCO3 (no compensation) = uncompensated respiratory alkalosis.

stem: PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) produces which physiological condition?
opts: Ventilator delivers full preset TV with every patient-triggered breath
Spontaneous tidal volume determined by patient's negative pressure generation
No breaths delivered without patient respiratory drive
Positive pressure maintained in the lungs at end of expiration
rat: PEEP maintains positive airway pressure throughout expiration, preventing alveolar collapse (atelectasis) and improving oxygenation by keeping alveoli open. It is measured in cm H2O and is an adjunct applied to mechanical breaths.
optRationales: Full preset TV with every triggered breath describes assist/control ventilation — not PEEP.
Spontaneous TV determined by negative pressure generation describes unassisted spontaneous breathing — not PEEP.
No breaths without respiratory drive describes controlled ventilation — not PEEP.
PEEP adds positive pressure at end expiration to prevent alveolar collapse and improve V/Q matching and oxygenation.

stem: Which statement should guide nursing care for a mechanically ventilated patient?
opts: Communication with intubated patients is often difficult and requires alternative strategies
Controlled ventilation is the preferred mode for most patients
Patients with COPD wean easily from mechanical ventilation
Wrist restraints are applied to all ventilated patients to prevent self-extubation
rat: An artificial airway prevents normal speech. The nurse must use alternative communication methods (lip reading, writing, picture boards, communication apps). Restraints are individualized decisions. COPD patients often have difficulty weaning. SIMV and A/C are the preferred modes — not controlled ventilation.
optRationales: The ETT or tracheostomy prevents normal speech — nurses must proactively establish alternative communication methods with ventilated patients.
Controlled ventilation is rarely used — SIMV and assist/control are the preferred modes as they allow patient participation.
COPD patients often have great difficulty weaning due to chronic hypercarbia, altered respiratory mechanics, and air trapping.
Restraints are an individualized clinical decision based on patient agitation and safety — not applied routinely to all ventilated patients.

stem: A patient is having difficulty weaning from mechanical ventilation. Which assessment finding is most likely contributing to the weaning failure?
rat: Hemoglobin of 8 g/dL significantly reduces oxygen-carrying capacity — inadequate oxygen delivery to muscles makes the increased work of spontaneous breathing unsustainable. CO 6 L/min, negative sputum culture, and WBC 8000 are all normal findings that would support weaning.
optRationales: CO of 6 L/min is normal (4-8 L/min) — adequate cardiac output supports weaning.
Hemoglobin 8 g/dL is low (normal 12-17 g/dL) — reduced oxygen-carrying capacity impairs ability to sustain spontaneous breathing and is a reversible cause of weaning failure.
Negative sputum culture indicates absence of lower respiratory infection — this supports weaning.
WBC 8000/mm³ is normal — absence of systemic infection supports weaning readiness.

stem: Post-cardiac surgery ICU patient has ABGs: pH 7.40, PaCO2 40, HCO3 24, PaO2 95, SpO2 97%, RR 20. How should the nurse interpret these values?
rat: All values fall within normal ranges: pH 7.35-7.45 ✓, PaCO2 35-45 ✓, HCO3 22-26 ✓, PaO2 80-100 ✓, SpO2 >95% ✓. These are entirely normal arterial blood gas values.
optRationales: Compensated metabolic acidosis would show low HCO3 with low PaCO2 as compensation — all values here are normal.
Metabolic alkalosis would show elevated HCO3 — HCO3 of 24 is normal.
All parameters are within normal range — pH 7.40, PaCO2 40, HCO3 24, PaO2 95, SpO2 97% are all normal.
Respiratory acidosis requires elevated PaCO2 and low pH — both are normal here.

stem: A post-cardiac surgery patient weaning on T-piece becomes restless with HR 110, RR 36, BP 156/98, 10 PVCs/min, elevated PAP, and pink frothy secretions. ABGs: pH 7.28, PaCO2 46, HCO3 22, PaO2 58, SpO2 88%. How should the nurse interpret these ABGs?
opts: Normal oxygenation with partially compensated metabolic acidosis
rat: PaO2 58 = hypoxemia (<80). pH 7.28 = acidosis. PaCO2 46 = elevated = respiratory cause. HCO3 22 = normal = no compensation. Uncompensated respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia — consistent with acute pulmonary edema/fluid overload.
optRationales: Respiratory alkalosis requires low PaCO2 — PaCO2 is elevated at 46 mm Hg.
PaO2 58 = hypoxemia, pH 7.28 = acidosis, PaCO2 46 = respiratory cause, HCO3 22 = normal (no compensation) = uncompensated respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia.
pH 7.28 and PaO2 58 are both abnormal — these are not normal values.
PaO2 58 indicates hypoxemia, not normal oxygenation. HCO3 22 is normal — no metabolic component.

stem: A post-cardiac surgery patient develops restlessness, HR 110, RR 36, elevated PAP, and pink frothy secretions. The nurse communicates with the physician. Which statement best reflects clinical understanding?
opts: 'May we order cardiac enzymes? This looks like a myocardial infarction.'
'The frequent PVCs are compromising cardiac output.'
'This looks like a hypertensive crisis — what medications would you like?'
rat: Pink frothy sputum, elevated PAP, bilateral crackles, and tachycardia are classic signs of acute pulmonary edema from fluid overload. The hypertension is secondary to the fluid overload and will resolve with treatment.
optRationales: There are no ECG changes or chest pain to suggest MI — the clinical picture is consistent with fluid overload, not infarction.
Pink frothy secretions, elevated PAP, crackles, and hemodynamic changes all point to acute fluid overload and pulmonary edema.
10 PVCs/min with adequate BP does not indicate compromised cardiac output — PVCs may be related to hypoxemia or surgery.
The hypertension is secondary to fluid overload — treating the underlying fluid excess will address the BP; antihypertensives alone miss the diagnosis.

stem: A ventilator high-pressure alarm sounds. The nurse cannot quickly identify the cause. SpO2 is dropping, HR and RR are increasing. What is the priority action?
opts: Ask respiratory therapy to get a new ventilator
Manually ventilate the patient and call respiratory therapy
rat: When the cause of a ventilator alarm cannot be rapidly identified and the patient is deteriorating, disconnect from the ventilator and manually ventilate with a bag-valve-mask while calling for the respiratory therapist. The patient's oxygenation takes priority over finding the cause.
optRationales: Getting a new ventilator takes time — the patient needs immediate ventilation now. This is determined after the problem is assessed.
The respiratory therapist — not the rapid response team — is the appropriate resource for ventilator troubleshooting.
Continuing to troubleshoot while the patient deteriorates is dangerous — if the cause cannot be found quickly, manual ventilation must begin.
Manual ventilation with BVM ensures the patient is oxygenated while the respiratory therapist troubleshoots the ventilator — the correct priority action.

stem: A patient on 15 cm H2O PEEP is being monitored. The nurse understands that high PEEP levels may cause which complication?
opts: Fluid overload from decreased venous return
High cardiac index from more efficient ventricular function
Hypoxemia from prolonged positive pressure at expiration
Low cardiac output from increased intrathoracic pressure
rat: High PEEP increases intrathoracic pressure, which compresses the vena cava and impedes venous return. Reduced preload decreases cardiac output. Optimal PEEP is the highest amount that improves oxygenation without compromising cardiac output.
optRationales: PEEP causes decreased venous return — but this results in decreased CO, not fluid overload.
PEEP typically decreases cardiac index by impairing venous return and preload — not increases it.
PEEP treats hypoxemia by preventing alveolar collapse — it does not cause hypoxemia.
High PEEP increases intrathoracic pressure → impedes venous return → decreased preload → decreased cardiac output. The key complication to monitor.

stem: What is the earliest cardiovascular sign of hypoxemia?
rat: Tachycardia is the earliest cardiovascular compensatory response to hypoxemia — the heart increases rate to maintain oxygen delivery. Dysrhythmias (like PVCs) occur later. Restlessness is the earliest neurological sign. Tachypnea is the earliest respiratory sign.
optRationales: Heart block is not an early sign of hypoxemia — dysrhythmias like PVCs may occur with prolonged hypoxemia but are not early cardiovascular signs.
Restlessness is the earliest neurological sign of hypoxemia — not a cardiovascular sign.
Tachycardia is the earliest cardiovascular compensatory response — the heart increases rate to maintain cardiac output and oxygen delivery.
Tachypnea is an early respiratory compensatory sign — but the question specifically asks for the cardiovascular system.

stem: The care team is considering a percutaneous tracheostomy for a difficult-to-wean patient. Which statement about tracheostomy is most accurate?
opts: Better outcomes result from tracheostomy within the first week of intubation
Percutaneous tracheostomy can be safely performed at the bedside by respiratory therapists
Operating room tracheostomy has fewer complications than bedside procedures
The greatest risk after percutaneous tracheostomy is accidental decannulation
raw: With percutaneous tracheostomy the trachea is not surgically sutured to the skin — if the tube is accidentally dislodged early after the procedure, reinsertion is difficult and the airway can be lost. This is the most significant unique risk of the percutaneous approach.
rat: With percutaneous tracheostomy the trachea is not surgically sutured to the skin — if the tube is accidentally dislodged early after the procedure, reinsertion is difficult and the airway can be lost. This is the most significant unique risk of the percutaneous approach.
optRationales: Optimal timing of tracheostomy is not clearly established — there is no strong evidence that within one week consistently produces better outcomes.
Percutaneous tracheostomies are performed by trained physicians at the bedside — not by respiratory therapists.
Bedside percutaneous tracheostomy is not associated with higher complication rates than operating room procedures when performed by trained physicians.
Accidental decannulation is the greatest risk because the trachea is not sutured to the skin — early dislodgement can result in airway loss.

stem: Why does the nurse assess the exhaled tidal volume (EVT) in a mechanically ventilated patient?
opts: To assess the level of PEEP
To compare delivered TV with prescribed TV
To determine the patient's work of breathing
rat: EVT is measured to ensure the patient is receiving the prescribed tidal volume. Volume can be lost through leaks in the ventilator circuit, around an underinflated ETT cuff, or around a chest tube. A significant discrepancy between set and exhaled TV indicates a leak requiring investigation.
optRationales: Tension pneumothorax is assessed clinically (absent breath sounds, hypotension, tracheal deviation) and with imaging — not by EVT.
PEEP is a set ventilator parameter measured directly — not assessed through EVT.
EVT is compared to prescribed TV to detect volume loss from circuit leaks, cuff underinflation, or chest tube air loss.
Work of breathing is assessed by measures such as respiratory rate, accessory muscle use, and negative inspiratory force — not EVT.

stem: The nurse responds to a high inspiratory pressure alarm on a ventilated patient. Which findings should the nurse assess for? Select all that apply.
opts: Patient coughing or attempting to talk
rat: High inspiratory pressure alarms are triggered by increased resistance or decreased compliance: coughing/agitation, kinked tubing, or secretions in the airway all increase peak inspiratory pressure. Disconnection causes a low exhaled volume alarm — not a high pressure alarm. Spontaneous breathing does not trigger pressure alarms.
optRationales: Coughing or fighting the ventilator increases airway pressure — a common cause of high pressure alarms.
Disconnection results in loss of volume return — it triggers a low exhaled tidal volume alarm, not a high pressure alarm.
Kinks in the tubing increase resistance to gas flow — this raises inspiratory pressure and triggers the alarm.
Secretions in the airway increase airway resistance — suctioning resolves this cause of high pressure alarms.
Spontaneous breathing between mechanical breaths does not trigger alarms — it is an expected finding in SIMV mode.

stem: Which factors may predispose a patient to respiratory acidosis? Select all that apply.
rat: Respiratory acidosis results from hypoventilation and CO2 retention. CNS depression (head injury, stroke) and sedative overdose both impair the respiratory drive, causing hypoventilation. Anxiety causes hyperventilation (respiratory alkalosis). DKA causes metabolic acidosis. NG suctioning removes HCl, causing metabolic alkalosis.
optRationales: Anxiety and fear cause hyperventilation — this blows off CO2 and causes respiratory alkalosis, not acidosis.
CNS depression impairs the respiratory center's drive to breathe — hypoventilation results in CO2 retention and respiratory acidosis.
Diabetic ketoacidosis produces ketoacids — this causes metabolic acidosis with compensatory respiratory alkalosis (Kussmaul breathing).
NG suctioning removes hydrochloric acid from the stomach — loss of H+ causes metabolic alkalosis.
Sedative overdose depresses the respiratory center — hypoventilation leads to CO2 retention and respiratory acidosis.

stem: After endotracheal intubation, which findings confirm correct ETT placement in the trachea? Select all that apply.
opts: Auscultation of air over the epigastrium
Equal bilateral breath sounds on auscultation
Tube position above the carina confirmed by chest x-ray
Positive CO2 detection via colorimetric or capnographic device
rat: Correct ETT placement is confirmed by bilateral breath sounds, chest x-ray showing tip above the carina (2-4 cm), and CO2 detection (CO2 comes from the lungs, not the esophagus). Epigastric air sounds indicate esophageal intubation. Tube fogging can occur with esophageal placement and is not reliable confirmation.
optRationales: Epigastric air sounds indicate esophageal intubation — the tube is in the stomach, not the trachea. This requires immediate removal.
Equal bilateral breath sounds confirm the tube is in the trachea above the carina — not in one mainstem bronchus.
Chest x-ray confirming the tip is 2-4 cm above the carina is the definitive confirmation of correct placement.
CO2 detection confirms tracheal placement — CO2 is present in exhaled air from the lungs but not from the esophagus.
Condensation (fogging) can occur with both tracheal and esophageal intubation — it is not a reliable indicator of correct placement.

stem: A ventilator alarm sounds while the nurse is charting outside the room. Place the following nursing actions in the correct priority order.
items: Check quickly for correctable causes of the alarm
Reconnect to mechanical ventilator and reassess patient
Go to the patient's bedside
Manually ventilate with BVM while calling respiratory therapy
rat: Priority: (1) Go to bedside immediately, (2) Quickly check for obvious fixable causes, (3) If not fixed in seconds — disconnect and manually ventilate while calling respiratory therapy, (4) Once problem resolved, reconnect and reassess.

stem: Place the steps of endotracheal intubation in the correct order.
items: Assess balloon on ETT for symmetry and leaks
Auscultate lung fields for bilateral expansion
Inflate the ETT balloon
Insert ETT with laryngoscope and blade
Suction the oropharynx
rat: Equipment is checked first (balloon integrity). Oropharynx is suctioned to visualize cords. Tube is inserted under direct laryngoscopy. Balloon is inflated to seal the airway. Position is confirmed by auscultating bilateral breath sounds and CO2 detection.

stem: During cardiopulmonary arrest before intubation is established, which method and oxygen concentration should the nurse use for ventilation?
rat: During resuscitation, 100% oxygen is administered via bag-valve-mask connected to a mask or ETT. The BVM delivers the highest FiO2 and allows controlled ventilation during CPR.
optRationales: BVM at 100% FiO2 is the standard during cardiac arrest — maximizes oxygen delivery during resuscitation.
50% FiO2 is inadequate during arrest — 100% oxygen is required to maximize tissue oxygenation.
Mouth-to-mask delivers a much lower FiO2 (~16-17%) — BVM with 100% O2 is preferred when available.
A non-rebreather mask requires spontaneous breathing to be effective — it cannot ventilate an apneic patient.

stem: Which device should laypersons use to treat lethal ventricular dysrhythmias outside a hospital setting?
rat: AEDs are designed for layperson use — they automatically analyze the rhythm and advise shock delivery for VF/pulseless VT. They are widely placed in public settings for early defibrillation before EMS arrival.
optRationales: AEDs automatically analyze rhythm and prompt the user to deliver a shock — designed specifically for layperson use to treat VF/VT.
CO2 detectors confirm ETT placement — they do not treat dysrhythmias.
Pocket masks provide ventilation support — they do not treat lethal dysrhythmias.
Transcutaneous pacemakers require training, equipment setup, and medical oversight — not appropriate for layperson use.

stem: When providing manual ventilations during a code with an advanced airway in place, at what rate should the nurse deliver breaths?
rat: Once an advanced airway is in place, ventilations are delivered asynchronously at 10-12 breaths/min without interrupting chest compressions. Compressions continue at 100-120/min simultaneously.
optRationales: 10-12 breaths/min is the correct rate for manual ventilation with an advanced airway — delivered asynchronously with continuous compressions.
Coordinating breaths with the fifth compression is the 2-rescuer BLS technique without an advanced airway — not the standard with an ETT.
20 breaths/min is too fast and causes hyperventilation, which reduces venous return and cerebral perfusion.
With an advanced airway in place, ventilations are given asynchronously — compressions should not be paused for ventilation.

stem: A cardiac monitor shows a flat line on an ICU patient with acute MI. What should the nurse do first?
rat: A flat line could be artifact, lead disconnection, or true asystole. The nurse must first assess the patient for unresponsiveness before initiating any intervention. Never treat the monitor — always assess the patient first.
optRationales: Epinephrine is administered during a confirmed cardiac arrest — not before the patient is assessed.
Chest compressions are initiated after confirming unresponsiveness and pulselessness — not as the first action.
Assessing unresponsiveness is always the first step — a flat line could be artifact from lead disconnection.
Defibrillation is for shockable rhythms (VF/pulseless VT) — asystole is not shockable, and the rhythm must be confirmed first.

stem: During anterior defibrillation, where should the nurse place the defibrillation pads/paddles?
opts: 2nd ICS left sternal border and 4th ICS left midclavicular line
2nd ICS right sternal border and 4th ICS left midaxillary line
2nd ICS right sternal border and 5th ICS left midaxillary line
4th ICS right sternal border and 5th ICS left midclavicular line
rat: Standard anterior defibrillation placement: one pad at the 2nd intercostal space right of the sternum (right clavicular area), and the other at the 5th intercostal space left midaxillary line (apex). This positions the heart between the two electrodes.
optRationales: The left sternal border is not correct for the first pad — it should be to the right of the sternum at the 2nd ICS.
The 4th ICS midaxillary placement is too high — the apical pad should be at the 5th ICS.
2nd ICS right sternal border (right clavicle area) and 5th ICS left midaxillary line (apex) — standard anterior defibrillation placement.
The right sternal border placement is too low at the 4th ICS — the right pad should be at the 2nd ICS.

stem: During synchronized cardioversion, the electrical charge is timed to coincide with which ECG wave?
rat: Cardioversion synchronizes the shock to the R wave (peak of QRS), avoiding delivery during the T wave (vulnerable period of repolarization). Shocking during the T wave can trigger ventricular fibrillation — the R-on-T phenomenon.
optRationales: The P wave represents atrial depolarization — synchronizing to it would not reliably avoid the vulnerable period.
Cardioversion synchronizes to the R wave — this ensures the shock avoids the T wave (vulnerable repolarization period) to prevent inducing VF.
The S wave is part of the QRS complex — synchronization targets the R wave peak specifically.
Delivering a shock on the T wave would cause R-on-T phenomenon, potentially triggering ventricular fibrillation — this is exactly what synchronization prevents.

stem: In the ACLS secondary survey, what does the 'D' in the A-B-C-D framework represent?
rat: The ACLS secondary survey D = Differential Diagnosis — identifying reversible causes of arrest (the H's and T's: hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion, hypo/hyperkalemia, hypothermia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis). Identifying and treating these can restore a perfusing rhythm.
optRationales: Defibrillation is part of the primary survey — the secondary survey D focuses on identifying underlying causes.
Differential diagnosis in the ACLS secondary survey involves searching for reversible causes of arrest (H's and T's) to guide specific treatment.
Diltiazem is used for rate control in SVT/AFib — it is not the D in the ACLS secondary survey.
DNR status is an ethical/legal consideration — it is not part of the ACLS secondary survey framework.

stem: A patient develops abrupt-onset supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). Which medication with a very short half-life is the initial drug of choice?
rat: Adenosine is the first-line drug for SVT — it temporarily blocks AV nodal conduction to terminate re-entrant SVT. Its onset is 10-40 seconds and duration only 1-2 minutes (extremely short half-life), so it must be administered rapidly via IV push followed by a saline flush.
optRationales: Adenosine has an onset of 10-40 seconds and duration of 1-2 minutes — the short half-life makes it ideal for SVT; must be given as rapid IV push.
Amiodarone is used for VF/pulseless VT and refractory SVT — it is not the initial drug of choice for SVT.
Diltiazem (calcium channel blocker) can be used for rate control in SVT but is not the initial drug of choice — adenosine comes first.
Procainamide is an antidysrhythmic for stable SVT unresponsive to adenosine — not the initial drug of choice.

stem: After defibrillating a patient in ventricular fibrillation and performing 2 minutes of CPR, what is the next action?
rat: After each 2-minute CPR cycle, assess the rhythm and check for a pulse. The rhythm assessment guides the next intervention — if still in VF, deliver another shock; if organized rhythm, check pulse. Continuous reassessment is fundamental to the ACLS algorithm.
optRationales: Amiodarone is given for VF not responding to CPR, defibrillation, and vasopressors — it is given after rhythm assessment confirms persistent VF, not before.
Lidocaine is an alternative antidysrhythmic for VF — it is given based on rhythm assessment, not before checking.
After each 2-minute CPR cycle, rhythm and pulse must be assessed to guide the next intervention — this is always the next step.
Transcutaneous pacing is for symptomatic bradycardia — not indicated in the VF algorithm after defibrillation.

stem: A patient has bradycardia (HR 40 bpm), frequent PVCs, and BP 85/50 mm Hg. Which drug should the nurse anticipate first?
rat: The PVCs are secondary to bradycardia. Atropine is the first-line drug for symptomatic bradycardia — it blocks vagal tone and increases heart rate. Dose: 0.5 mg IV every 3-5 minutes up to 3 mg. Lidocaine would suppress the compensatory PVCs and worsen conduction.
optRationales: Atropine is first-line for symptomatic bradycardia — increasing the heart rate will resolve the bradycardia-induced PVCs.
Dopamine is used after atropine fails or for hypotension after hypovolemia is corrected — not the first drug here.
Lidocaine suppresses ventricular conduction — giving it for bradycardia-induced PVCs could worsen the bradycardia and hemodynamic instability.
Transcutaneous pacing is used when atropine fails or is contraindicated (e.g., 2nd/3rd degree block) — atropine comes first.

stem: A monitor technician calls the nurse stat about a patient showing a rapid chaotic rhythm resembling VT. What is the nurse's first action?
opts: Go to the patient's bedside and assess immediately
Go to the nurses' station to review the rhythm strip
Take the crash cart to the room
rat: Never treat the monitor — always assess the patient first. The nurse must go directly to the bedside to check for responsiveness and pulse. The rhythm could be artifact. If the patient is confirmed pulseless, then call the code and begin CPR.
optRationales: Calling a code before assessing the patient is premature — the rhythm could be artifact or the patient could be stable.
Going directly to the bedside to assess the patient is always the first action — confirm the clinical picture before any intervention.
Going to the nurses' station first delays patient assessment — the nurse must go directly to the patient.
Taking the crash cart to the room is appropriate preparation but should happen concurrently with or after assessing the patient — not before.

stem: Which clinical scenario is an emergency indication for a transcutaneous pacemaker?
opts: Bradycardia HR 50 bpm with hypotension and syncope
rat: Transcutaneous pacing is indicated for symptomatic bradycardia unresponsive to atropine — symptoms include hypotension, altered mental status, angina, and pulmonary edema. This patient with HR 50 and hypotension plus syncope is symptomatic. Asystole and SVT are not indications for transcutaneous pacing.
optRationales: Asystole has a very poor prognosis — transcutaneous pacing is generally ineffective for true asystole and is not the primary intervention.
Bradycardia with normal BP and alert mental status is asymptomatic — monitoring and atropine trial are appropriate before pacing.
Bradycardia with hypotension and syncope = symptomatic bradycardia — transcutaneous pacing is indicated when atropine fails.
SVT with hypotension requires synchronized cardioversion — transcutaneous pacing is for bradyarrhythmias, not tachyarrhythmias.

stem: An inferior wall MI patient develops symptomatic bradycardia with trigeminal PVCs. Which drug should the nurse prepare?
rat: Symptomatic bradycardia is treated with atropine first — it increases heart rate by reducing vagal tone. The PVCs are secondary to bradycardia and will resolve when the rate increases. Lidocaine would suppress conduction and worsen bradycardia.
optRationales: Amiodarone is used for VF, pulseless VT, or refractory dysrhythmias — not for symptomatic bradycardia.
Atropine is the first-line drug for symptomatic bradycardia — increases heart rate by blocking vagal tone, resolving the bradycardia-induced PVCs.
Lidocaine suppresses ventricular ectopy but also depresses conduction — contraindicated in bradycardia as it worsens the rate.
Magnesium is used for torsades de pointes, hypomagnesemia, or refractory VF — not indicated for symptomatic bradycardia.

stem: A patient develops frequent ventricular ectopy. Which drug should the nurse prepare to administer?
rat: Lidocaine is a Class IB antidysrhythmic that suppresses ventricular ectopic activity by stabilizing the cell membrane and raising the threshold for depolarization. It is the drug of choice for ventricular ectopy.
optRationales: Adenosine blocks AV nodal conduction — it is used for SVT, not ventricular ectopy.
Atropine increases heart rate by blocking vagal tone — it is used for bradycardia, not ventricular ectopy.
Lidocaine suppresses ventricular ectopic activity by stabilizing cardiac cell membranes — the correct drug for frequent PVCs/ventricular ectopy.
Magnesium is used for torsades de pointes or refractory VF — not the drug of choice for ventricular ectopy.

stem: A patient requires a transcutaneous pacemaker until a transvenous pacemaker can be placed. What is the most appropriate nursing intervention?
opts: Apply conductive gel to the skin
Set milliamperes 2 mA below the capture threshold
rat: Transcutaneous pacing stimulates skeletal muscles as well as cardiac muscle, causing a tingling, twitching, or thumping sensation ranging from uncomfortable to intolerable. Sedation and analgesia are essential for any alert patient receiving transcutaneous pacing.
optRationales: Transcutaneous pacing uses adhesive electrode pads — conductive gel is used for paddle-based defibrillation, not transcutaneous pacing pads.
Transcutaneous pacing causes significant discomfort from skeletal muscle stimulation — sedation and analgesia are mandatory for alert patients.
Rechecking leads is appropriate before initiating pacing but is not the most important nursing intervention once pacing is established.
The milliamperes should be set above the capture threshold — set below capture would result in failure to pace.

stem: Arterial blood gas analysis must be obtained before administering which medication?
rat: Sodium bicarbonate dosing must be guided by ABG results — specifically the pH and base deficit/bicarbonate level. Blind administration can cause metabolic alkalosis, paradoxical intracellular acidosis, and impaired oxygen delivery. ABG-guided dosing prevents over- or under-correction.
optRationales: Calcium chloride is given empirically for hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, or calcium channel blocker toxicity — ABG analysis is not required before administration.
Magnesium sulfate is dosed based on serum magnesium levels — not ABG analysis.
Potassium replacement is guided by serum potassium levels and urine output — not ABG analysis.
Sodium bicarbonate must be guided by ABG base deficit or bicarbonate concentration — prevents iatrogenic alkalosis from empiric administration.

stem: Which intravenous fluid is preferred during resuscitation efforts?
rat: Normal saline is the preferred IV fluid during resuscitation because it expands intravascular volume effectively. Dextrose-containing solutions can cause hyperglycemia (worsens neurological outcomes post-arrest) and do not expand intravascular volume as effectively.
optRationales: D5W 0.45 NS contains dextrose — hyperglycemia worsens neurological outcomes after cardiac arrest and this is not preferred.
D5W is hypotonic and distributes into cells rather than staying in the intravascular space — poor choice for volume expansion during resuscitation.
Dopamine is a vasopressor — it is used for hemodynamic support, not as a primary resuscitation fluid.
Normal saline expands intravascular volume, does not cause hyperglycemia, and is the preferred fluid during cardiac resuscitation.

stem: A 90-year-old nursing home patient with severe pneumonia is admitted with no living will or healthcare surrogate documentation. If the patient arrests, what should the nurse do?
opts: Activate the code team but initiate a 'slow code'
Call the nursing home to determine wishes
Initiate CPR for 5 minutes then cease
rat: Without a written physician order to withhold resuscitative measures (DNR order), full resuscitation must be initiated. 'Slow codes' are ethically impermissible. The nurse cannot independently limit resuscitation — a valid DNR order or surrogate decision is required.
optRationales: 'Slow codes' are ethically unacceptable — they create an illusion of resuscitation while deliberately providing substandard care, violating patient rights.
Calling the nursing home to gather information is appropriate after initiating resuscitation — it cannot delay or replace immediate CPR without a DNR order.
Arbitrarily stopping CPR after 5 minutes without a DNR order is not ethically or legally permissible.
Without a written DNR or advance directive, full resuscitation must be initiated — the nurse cannot independently withhold resuscitative efforts.

stem: A post-MVA patient presents with dyspnea, chest pain, absent breath sounds on the left, and tracheal deviation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
rat: Tension pneumothorax classic triad: absent breath sounds on the affected side, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, and hemodynamic compromise. Air enters the pleural space but cannot escape — increasing pressure collapses the lung and shifts the mediastinum.
optRationales: Pericardial tamponade presents with Beck's triad: hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and JVD — not absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation.
Symptomatic bradycardia is a cardiac rate problem — not a cause of absent breath sounds and tracheal shift.
Absent unilateral breath sounds + tracheal deviation away from the affected side after trauma = tension pneumothorax — requires immediate needle decompression.
Unstable tachycardia is a cardiac rhythm problem — not associated with absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation.

stem: A patient has PEA caused by pericardial tamponade. What is the most appropriate treatment?
rat: Post-cardiac surgery pericardial tamponade causing PEA requires emergency resternotomy to decompress the cardiac tamponade and control bleeding. Pericardiocentesis is the standard approach for non-surgical tamponade, but in the post-cardiac surgery setting resternotomy is required.
optRationales: Atropine treats bradycardia by blocking vagal tone — it does not address the mechanical compression from tamponade.
Chest tube placement decompresses pneumothorax — tamponade requires pericardial decompression, not pleural.
Resternotomy controls the bleeding around the heart and relieves cardiac compression from tamponade in the post-cardiac surgery patient.
Transcutaneous pacing treats bradycardia — it cannot restore cardiac output in the presence of mechanical compression from tamponade.

stem: What is the primary rationale for targeted temperature management (therapeutic hypothermia) after cardiac arrest?
opts: Hypothermia decreases metabolic rate 6-7% per degree Celsius decrease
Lower body temperatures benefit patients with low blood pressure
Lower body temperature leads to decreased oxygen delivery
rat: Targeted temperature management to 32-34°C reduces the metabolic rate by 6-7% per °C decrease, protecting the brain from ischemic injury after cardiac arrest. Reduced metabolic demand decreases secondary neuronal injury during the post-arrest period.
optRationales: Reducing metabolic rate 6-7% per degree Celsius protects neurons from post-arrest ischemia — the primary rationale for therapeutic hypothermia.
Hypothermia can actually cause hemodynamic instability — it is not indicated for hypotension and does not benefit low BP patients.
40°C is hyperthermia — post-arrest fever worsens neurological outcomes; the target is 32-34°C for neuroprotection.
Decreased oxygen delivery would worsen — not improve — neurological outcomes. Hypothermia reduces oxygen demand, not delivery.

stem: A transcutaneous pacemaker is in place. The nurse sees pacemaker spikes followed by QRS complexes on the monitor. What must the nurse do to confirm the pacemaker is working effectively?
rat: Electrical capture (spikes followed by QRS) confirms electrical effectiveness. Mechanical effectiveness — whether the electrical activity produces a mechanical contraction — is confirmed only by palpating a pulse. Electrical capture without a pulse is pulseless electrical activity.
optRationales: A 12-lead ECG confirms the paced rhythm morphology — but does not confirm mechanical capture (pulse generation).
Pacemaker interrogation is performed for permanent implanted devices — transcutaneous pacing effectiveness is assessed clinically.
Palpating the pulse confirms mechanical capture — electrical spikes and QRS complexes on the monitor confirm only electrical capture, not mechanical.
A monitor strip confirms electrical activity — it cannot confirm that the heart is generating adequate mechanical output.

stem: A patient was converted from VT with pulse to sinus rhythm but is now hypotensive. Which treatments are appropriate? Select all that apply.
rat: Post-conversion hypotension is treated first with IV fluids (normal saline) for volume resuscitation. If hypotension persists after fluid resuscitation, dopamine infusion is indicated as a vasopressor/inotrope. Adenosine, magnesium, and sodium bicarbonate have no role in treating post-conversion hypotension.
optRationales: Adenosine blocks AV conduction for SVT — not indicated for post-conversion hypotension.
Dopamine is indicated for hypotension after hypovolemia has been corrected — appropriate second-line treatment.
Magnesium is used for torsades de pointes or hypomagnesemia — not for post-conversion hypotension.
Normal saline for volume resuscitation is the first-line treatment for post-conversion hypotension.
Sodium bicarbonate corrects metabolic acidosis — not indicated for hemodynamic hypotension.

stem: A patient has symptomatic bradycardia (HR 39 bpm) with PVCs, lethargy, and dizziness. Which treatments are acceptable? Select all that apply.
rat: Symptomatic bradycardia is treated with atropine (first-line), transcutaneous pacing (if atropine fails), and epinephrine infusion (alternative). Lidocaine depresses conduction and is contraindicated — it would worsen bradycardia. Magnesium is not indicated for bradycardia.
optRationales: Atropine 0.5 mg IV every 3-5 min (max 3 mg) is the first-line drug for symptomatic bradycardia.
Epinephrine infusion (2-10 mcg/min) is an acceptable alternative when atropine and pacing are insufficient.
Lidocaine depresses ventricular conduction — contraindicated in bradycardia as it can worsen rate and hemodynamic status.
Transcutaneous pacing is indicated for symptomatic bradycardia unresponsive to atropine — appropriate treatment.
Magnesium sulfate is used for torsades de pointes or hypomagnesemia — not indicated for bradycardia management.

stem: Ventricular fibrillation should initially be treated with which of the following? Select all that apply.
opts: Atropine 1 mg then defibrillation at 200 J
Defibrillation at 200 J with biphasic defibrillator
Defibrillation at 360 J with monophasic defibrillator
rat: VF is treated with immediate unsynchronized defibrillation. Biphasic: 120-200 J (use 200 J if unknown). Monophasic: 360 J. Dobutamine and dopamine are not used for VF. Atropine is not used in VF — it is for bradycardia.
optRationales: Dobutamine is an inotrope for cardiogenic shock — not used to treat VF.
Atropine is for bradycardia — not indicated in the VF algorithm. The initial energy for VF is not 200 J for monophasic.
Biphasic defibrillation at 120-200 J (200 J if dose unknown) is the correct initial treatment for VF with a biphasic defibrillator.
Monophasic defibrillation at 360 J is the correct initial energy for VF with a monophasic defibrillator.
Dopamine infusion is for post-resuscitation hemodynamic support — not for treating active VF.

stem: Which code medications can be safely administered via endotracheal tube when IV access is unavailable? Select all that apply.
rat: The mnemonic NAVEL/LATE describes ETT-administered drugs: Atropine, Epinephrine, Lidocaine, Vasopressin (and Naloxone). Adenosine requires rapid IV push for effectiveness — its mechanism depends on direct cardiac delivery and is not effective via ETT.
optRationales: Adenosine must be delivered via rapid IV push directly into circulation — it is not effective via ETT due to its mechanism and pharmacokinetics.
Atropine can be administered via ETT when IV access is unavailable — use 2-3x the IV dose.
Epinephrine can be administered via ETT — use 2-3x the IV dose diluted in 10 mL normal saline.
Vasopressin can be administered via ETT as an alternative to epinephrine during cardiac arrest.
Lidocaine can be administered via ETT for ventricular dysrhythmias when IV access is unavailable.

stem: Which statements about defibrillation are correct? Select all that apply.
opts: Early defibrillation is recommended before other interventions when indicated
Hands-off defibrillation eliminates the need to clear personnel from the patient
Defibrillation shocks are delivered without synchronization
Pads can be placed anteriorly and posteriorly on the chest
rat: Early unsynchronized defibrillation is the priority for VF/pulseless VT. Pads can be placed anterior-posterior as an alternative to anterior placement. All personnel must clear the patient regardless of method. Defibrillators vary by manufacturer and nurses must be familiar with their unit's model.
optRationales: Early defibrillation is the highest priority for VF/pulseless VT — survival rates decrease 7-10% for every minute without defibrillation.
All personnel must clear the patient during shock delivery regardless of the defibrillation method — contact during shock delivery is dangerous.
Defibrillation shocks are unsynchronized — synchronization is used only for cardioversion to avoid the T wave vulnerable period.
Anteroposterior pad placement is an acceptable alternative to the standard anterior placement — used when anterior approach is not feasible.
Defibrillators come in many different models — nurses must be familiar with the specific model on their unit, not assume standardization.

stem: Which are appropriate post-resuscitation goals? Select all that apply.
rat: Post-resuscitation care focuses on optimizing tissue perfusion: airway maintenance, hemodynamic stability, oxygenation, and dysrhythmia control. Weaning oxygen and early ambulation are long-term rehabilitation goals — not immediate post-resuscitation priorities.
optRationales: Dysrhythmia control prevents re-arrest — a core post-resuscitation goal.
Airway maintenance ensures oxygenation and ventilation — a primary post-resuscitation goal.
Blood pressure maintenance ensures adequate organ perfusion — a core post-resuscitation goal.
Oxygen weaning is a long-term goal — post-resuscitation patients need maximized oxygenation, not oxygen reduction.
Early ambulation is a rehabilitation goal — not an immediate post-resuscitation priority.

stem: Which items must be documented as part of the cardiopulmonary arrest record? Select all that apply.
opts: Defibrillation times, joules delivered, and outcomes
Rhythm strips of cardiac rhythms noted during the code
Signatures of recorder and all personnel involved
rat: Code documentation must include: all medication times and doses, defibrillation times and energies, rhythm strips, IV access sites and fluids, intubation details, and signatures of all involved personnel. Equipment model numbers are not required documentation.
optRationales: Defibrillator model number is not required in code documentation — only the joules delivered and outcomes.
Medication times, doses, and routes are mandatory code documentation.
Defibrillation times, energy levels, and patient response must be documented for each shock delivered.
Rhythm strips document the cardiac events and patient response to interventions — required documentation.
Signatures of the recorder and all code team members are required — establishes accountability.

stem: Which are recognized benefits of having family members present during resuscitation? Select all that apply.
opts: Family sees that everything possible is being done
Sustains patient-family relationships during the event
Provides opportunity to request organ donation
rat: Family presence during resuscitation benefits include: facilitating grief, witnessing that all efforts were made, maintaining the patient-family bond, and achieving closure. Using the opportunity to solicit organ donation is not appropriate — this is ethically and legally a separate, later conversation.
optRationales: Witnessing the resuscitation helps families begin processing their grief — a recognized psychological benefit.
Seeing the team's efforts reassures families that everything possible was done — reduces later doubt and regret.
Remaining present maintains the patient-family relationship during the patient's final moments.
Organ donation discussions should not occur during resuscitation — this is inappropriate and a separate process.
