Brown-Séquard syndrome — ipsilateral motor loss and contralateral pain/temperature loss
Posterior cord syndrome — loss of proprioception and vibration sensation with preserved motor function
optRationales: Anterior cord syndrome results from injury to the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord — typically from flexion injury or anterior spinal artery compromise. It produces loss of motor function AND pain/temperature sensation below the injury, but preserves proprioception and vibration (dorsal columns intact). The pattern here (upper extremity weakness greater than lower) is not consistent with anterior cord syndrome.

Central cord syndrome is the most common incomplete SCI pattern. It results from hyperextension injury (common in elderly patients with cervical spondylosis) damaging the central gray matter. The cervical cord is arranged somatotopically with upper extremity fibers more central — so central damage disproportionately affects arms more than legs. Classic presentation: bilateral upper extremity weakness > lower extremity weakness, bladder dysfunction (urinary retention), and variable sensory loss below injury level. The patient often retains some leg function and can walk, while arms are significantly impaired.

Brown-Séquard syndrome results from hemisection of the cord (penetrating injury). It produces ipsilateral motor paralysis and ipsilateral loss of proprioception/vibration, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation (these fibers cross at the level of entry). This bilateral presentation is not Brown-Séquard.

Posterior cord syndrome is the rarest incomplete SCI — it affects the dorsal columns. Motor function is intact but proprioception and vibration are lost, causing profound ataxia. This patient has motor weakness, ruling out posterior cord syndrome.
rat: Incomplete SCI syndromes — the four patterns: Central cord syndrome (most common): hyperextension injury, upper extremity > lower extremity weakness, bladder dysfunction, variable sensory loss. Best prognosis for recovery of the incomplete syndromes. Anterior cord syndrome: flexion or vascular injury, complete motor and pain/temperature loss below injury, dorsal columns preserved. Poor prognosis — least likely to recover motor function. Brown-Séquard syndrome: hemisection (penetrating), ipsilateral motor loss + contralateral pain/temperature loss. Best prognosis overall. Posterior cord syndrome: rarest, dorsal column injury, ataxia with preserved motor and pain/temperature. Nursing care in central cord syndrome: immobilization, monitoring for neurogenic shock (bradycardia + hypotension), maintaining MAP ≥85–90 mmHg for spinal cord perfusion, bladder management (intermittent catheterization for retention), DVT prophylaxis, skin integrity.

stem: A nurse is caring for a patient with central cord syndrome from a cervical hyperextension injury. Which clinical findings are consistent with this diagnosis? Select all that apply.
opts: Weakness in both arms greater than both legs
Complete loss of all motor and sensory function below C5
Variable sensory impairment below the level of injury
History of a fall with forced neck hyperextension in an older adult with cervical spondylosis
rat: Central cord syndrome characteristics: Bilateral upper extremity weakness greater than lower extremity weakness (option A) — the hallmark finding. The corticospinal tracts are arranged with cervical fibers running most centrally; central cord damage preferentially damages the upper extremity pathways while partially sparing the peripheral lower extremity fibers. Urinary retention (option B) — bladder dysfunction is nearly universal in central cord syndrome; the autonomic pathways controlling the bladder run centrally and are disrupted. Intermittent catheterization is required. Variable sensory impairment (option D) — sensory loss is incomplete and variable; patients often retain some sensation but may have altered temperature, pain, or proprioception below the injury. Mechanism: hyperextension in elderly patients with cervical spondylosis (option E) — the narrowed canal from degenerative changes leaves little room; hyperextension pinches the cord centrally. Complete loss of all function (option C) describes a complete SCI — central cord syndrome is an INCOMPLETE injury by definition. Patients retain some function below the level of injury, which is what distinguishes incomplete from complete SCI.

stem: A patient with an acute exacerbation of COPD has a respiratory rate of 32, SpO2 88%, and is using accessory muscles. ABG shows pH 7.29, PaCO2 58 mmHg, PaO2 56 mmHg. The provider orders non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP). The nurse understands BiPAP is preferred over immediate intubation in this patient because:
opts: BiPAP delivers a higher FiO2 than mechanical ventilation and is therefore more effective for COPD
BiPAP avoids the risks of intubation while providing inspiratory support to reduce work of breathing and assist CO2 elimination, buying time for bronchodilators to work
BiPAP is the only ventilation modality appropriate for COPD patients because mechanical ventilation causes oxygen toxicity
BiPAP is used because COPD patients always have a hypoxic drive and supplemental oxygen should be minimized
optRationales: BiPAP does not inherently deliver higher FiO2 than mechanical ventilation — both can be titrated. Mechanical ventilation can deliver up to 100% FiO2 if needed. The advantage of BiPAP is not FiO2 delivery but avoidance of invasive intubation and its associated complications.

Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV/BiPAP) provides two levels of pressure support: IPAP (inspiratory positive airway pressure) assists each breath, reducing the work of breathing and helping eliminate CO2; EPAP (expiratory positive airway pressure) acts like PEEP, preventing alveolar collapse and improving oxygenation. In acute COPD exacerbation, BiPAP reduces CO2, improves pH, decreases respiratory muscle fatigue, and avoids intubation risks (VAP, airway trauma, prolonged sedation). Evidence shows BiPAP reduces intubation rates and mortality in COPD exacerbation when started early.

Mechanical ventilation is absolutely used in COPD when BiPAP fails or is contraindicated (unconscious patient, inability to protect airway, hemodynamic instability). The statement that MV 'always causes oxygen toxicity' is false — oxygen is titrated carefully on MV just as with any delivery system.

The hypoxic drive concept (COPD patients rely on low O2 to breathe) is largely a myth that has been overstated. COPD patients should still receive oxygen to target SpO2 88–92% to avoid hypoxia. Withholding oxygen to 'protect hypoxic drive' in a severely hypoxic patient is dangerous and not evidence-based.
rat: BiPAP (Bilevel Positive Airway Pressure) for acute COPD exacerbation: IPAP assists inspiration → reduces work of breathing, augments tidal volume, helps eliminate CO2. EPAP prevents expiratory alveolar collapse, improves V/Q matching, and boosts oxygenation. Benefits over intubation: preserves the patient's airway reflexes, avoids VAP risk, allows speech and oral medications, easier to wean. Indications for BiPAP in COPD: moderate-severe dyspnea, respiratory acidosis (pH 7.25–7.35), PaCO2 elevated and rising. Contraindications: unconscious/unable to protect airway, vomiting, facial trauma, hemodynamic instability. If BiPAP fails (pH continues to fall, patient tires, SpO2 cannot be maintained) — intubation is required. Settings: IPAP typically 10–20 cmH2O; EPAP 4–8 cmH2O; FiO2 titrated to SpO2 88–92% in COPD.

stem: A patient on BiPAP removes the mask repeatedly, stating 'I can't breathe with this thing on.' SpO2 is 91%, RR 26. Which nursing intervention is the priority?
opts: Remove BiPAP and apply a simple face mask at 6L/min — the patient's comfort is the priority
Restrain the patient's hands to prevent mask removal — adherence is essential for BiPAP to work
Reassess mask fit, reapply with coaching on breathing with the device, and address anxiety — BiPAP adherence is essential but requires patient cooperation
Increase IPAP to 20 cmH2O immediately — higher pressure will force the patient to tolerate the mask
optRationales: Switching to a simple face mask at 6L/min abandons BiPAP before optimizing adherence. This patient's respiratory status (RR 26, SpO2 91%) still benefits from ventilatory support. BiPAP should be trialed and optimized before downgrading — simple O2 delivery will not address the CO2 retention driving the dyspnea.

Restraining a patient is a last resort requiring clinical justification and physician order. It does not address the underlying problem — the patient is likely experiencing claustrophobia, mask discomfort, or anxiety from the device. Restraint without addressing the root cause will worsen agitation and is not first-line.

Patient intolerance is the most common reason BiPAP fails. Priority nursing interventions: check mask fit (air leaks worsen discomfort and reduce effectiveness), reapply the mask while the patient is sitting upright, coach the patient through breathing synchronously with the machine, explain what the device is doing, address anxiety (reassurance before pharmacologic sedation), consider anxiolytics only if refractory agitation prevents adherence. Starting pressures lower and titrating up improves tolerance. BiPAP requires a cooperative patient — coaching is essential.

Increasing IPAP to maximum without the patient's cooperation will worsen intolerance, increase air leak around the mask, and potentially cause aerophagia (air swallowing). Pressure adjustments are made incrementally based on patient response and blood gas values, not to force compliance.
rat: BiPAP adherence and nursing management: Patient intolerance is the #1 cause of BiPAP failure. Strategies to improve adherence: proper mask sizing and fitting (full face mask preferred in acute respiratory failure — prevents mouth breathing bypassing the system), start at lower pressures and titrate up, coach patient to breathe with the machine rather than fighting it, explain what the machine is doing and why, keep patient in upright position (30–45 degrees), address anxiety (coaching first, then consider low-dose anxiolytic if refractory), use chin straps for mouth breathers, check for air leaks around mask. Signs BiPAP is working: decreasing RR, improving SpO2, rising pH, decreasing PaCO2, subjective improvement in dyspnea. BiPAP failure requiring intubation: deteriorating pH despite 1–2 hours of BiPAP, decreasing LOC, inability to maintain airway, hemodynamic instability.

stem: A patient has a chest tube in place following a left-sided pneumothorax. During shift assessment the nurse observes the water-seal chamber. Which findings indicate the chest tube is functioning correctly? Select all that apply.
opts: Tidaling — the water level in the water-seal chamber rises with inspiration and falls with expiration
Continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber throughout the respiratory cycle
Fluctuation of fluid in the drainage tubing with respiratory effort
No air leak — gentle bubbling in the water-seal chamber only during forced expiration or coughing
Drainage tubing free of dependent loops and kinks
rat: Chest tube water-seal chamber assessment: Tidaling (option A) is NORMAL and expected — water rises with inspiration (negative intrathoracic pressure pulls water up) and falls with expiration. Tidaling confirms the system is patent and connected to the pleural space. If tidaling stops, the lung has re-expanded (expected outcome) OR the tube is kinked/obstructed. Gentle bubbling during coughing/forced expiration only (option D) — acceptable finding indicating a small air leak that is resolving. Continuous constant bubbling throughout the respiratory cycle (option B) is ABNORMAL — indicates a persistent large air leak from the lung OR a loose connection in the tubing system. The nurse should check all connections first. Drainage tubing free of loops and kinks (option E) — essential for proper drainage; dependent loops trap fluid and create back-pressure, impairing drainage. Option C (fluctuation in drainage tubing) describes tidaling and is partially correct, but the most precise correct description is option A. Management: never clamp a chest tube without a specific order (risk of tension pneumothorax if lung is still leaking); keep collection system below chest level; assess drainage color and amount hourly in acute phase.

stem: A nurse is monitoring a patient with a chest tube for drainage of a pleural effusion. The water-seal chamber shows continuous vigorous bubbling throughout the entire respiratory cycle. The tubing connections are all tight and intact. Which complication does the nurse suspect?
opts: The lung has fully re-expanded and the chest tube is ready to be removed
Tidaling — a normal finding indicating the chest tube is patent
The suction level is set too high and should be decreased
A persistent air leak from the lung parenchyma into the pleural space
optRationales: Lung re-expansion causes tidaling to STOP (no more pressure differential once the lung fills the space) and bubbling to CEASE. Full re-expansion does not cause continuous vigorous bubbling — it produces the absence of tidaling and bubbling.

Tidaling is a gentle rhythmic rise and fall of the water level synchronized with breathing — not continuous vigorous bubbling. Tidaling is a normal, expected finding. Continuous bubbling is distinctly different from tidaling and is always abnormal after connections are confirmed intact.

The suction chamber controls suction level — increasing or decreasing suction affects the suction chamber, not the water-seal chamber bubbling pattern. The water-seal chamber reflects air leaking from the patient's pleural space, not suction settings.

Continuous vigorous bubbling in the water-seal chamber throughout the respiratory cycle — after confirming all connections are secure — indicates air is continuously entering the pleural space and escaping through the water seal. This means there is a persistent air leak from the lung itself (bronchopleural fistula, persistent pneumothorax with ongoing air leak, or alveolar tear). The provider must be notified. If the bubbling is new and sudden, check for disconnected tubing first — a disconnected tube causes vigorous bubbling from room air entering the system.
rat: Chest tube water-seal chamber bubbling assessment: Normal (expected): Tidaling only — rhythmic water level changes with breathing. Acceptable: Gentle bubbling during coughing or forced expiration only — small resolving air leak. Abnormal — requires action: Continuous vigorous bubbling = persistent air leak from lung. First: check ALL connections and tubing for disconnection or loose fittings. If connections intact → air leak from lung parenchyma (bronchopleural fistula, ongoing pneumothorax). Notify provider. No tidaling AND no bubbling: either lung has fully re-expanded (expected goal) OR tube is kinked/clotted/malpositioned. Assess patient, check tube, chest X-ray may be ordered. Nursing priority: never clamp a bubbling chest tube (can cause tension pneumothorax). Document drainage color (serous, serosanguineous, bloody), amount, and any changes in bubbling pattern every shift.

stem: A patient with type 2 respiratory failure from COPD exacerbation is started on BiPAP with IPAP 12/EPAP 5. After 90 minutes, ABG shows pH 7.32, PaCO2 52 mmHg (improved from 65), PaO2 72 mmHg. The patient is more comfortable, RR 20. The nurse interprets these findings as indicating:
opts: BiPAP is working — pH, PaCO2, and PaO2 are all trending in the right direction; continue current settings and reassess
BiPAP is failing — pH is still below normal and the patient should be intubated immediately
The FiO2 should be increased to 100% to normalize PaO2 above 80 mmHg in this COPD patient
The EPAP should be decreased to zero — the expiratory pressure is preventing CO2 elimination
optRationales: BiPAP effectiveness is evaluated by trending — not by whether values have normalized in 90 minutes. This patient shows all positive indicators: pH rising (less acidemic), PaCO2 falling (better ventilation), PaO2 improving, RR decreasing, and subjective improvement. Continue current settings and reassess in 1–2 hours with repeat ABG. Goals in COPD exacerbation: pH >7.35, PaCO2 returning toward patient's baseline (COPD patients often have chronically elevated CO2), SpO2 88–92%.

pH 7.32 is still acidemic but it has improved from the pre-BiPAP value. PaCO2 improved from 65 to 52 mmHg — CO2 is being eliminated. The patient is more comfortable and RR has decreased. These are all positive trends indicating BiPAP is working. Immediate intubation is not warranted — BiPAP should continue with ongoing monitoring.

Targeting PaO2 >80 mmHg in a COPD patient with chronic hypercapnia is inappropriate — and using 100% FiO2 risks further suppressing respiratory drive and worsening CO2 retention through the Haldane effect (O2 displaces CO2 from hemoglobin). Target SpO2 88–92% (PaO2 ~55–75 mmHg) in COPD.

EPAP (expiratory positive airway pressure) acts like PEEP — it prevents alveolar collapse, counteracts auto-PEEP in COPD (air trapping), and improves oxygenation. Reducing EPAP to zero would remove this benefit and worsen gas exchange. EPAP does not impair CO2 elimination — that is driven by the IPAP-EPAP pressure difference (pressure support).
rat: Monitoring BiPAP effectiveness in COPD exacerbation: assess at 1–2 hours with repeat ABG. Signs of success: pH increasing toward >7.35, PaCO2 decreasing toward patient's baseline, PaO2 improving, RR decreasing, decreased accessory muscle use, patient more comfortable. Goals for COPD specifically: SpO2 88–92% (not 95–100%), pH >7.35, PaCO2 at or near patient's baseline (often 45–60 in COPD patients chronically). Signs of BiPAP failure requiring intubation: pH continues to fall despite 2 hours of BiPAP, PaCO2 continues to rise, decreasing LOC, hemodynamic instability, patient cannot cooperate with mask. BiPAP settings: IPAP 10–20 cmH2O (provides ventilatory support), EPAP 4–8 cmH2O (provides PEEP effect, counters auto-PEEP). Pressure support = IPAP minus EPAP.

stem: A patient's chest tube drainage suddenly increases from 50 mL/hr to 250 mL/hr of bright red blood over the past hour following thoracic surgery. The nurse's priority action is to:
opts: Clamp the chest tube to prevent further blood loss
Notify the provider immediately — this volume and character of drainage suggests hemorrhage requiring urgent evaluation
Document the finding and reassess in one hour — postoperative chest tube drainage is expected
Increase the suction on the chest tube system to improve drainage
optRationales: Clamping a chest tube is dangerous and generally contraindicated without a specific physician order — it can cause tension pneumothorax if air is leaking, and it does not stop internal hemorrhage. The source of bleeding is inside the chest, not in the tube itself.

A sudden increase to 250 mL/hr of bright red blood indicates active hemorrhage — postoperative bleeding from a vessel, anastomosis, or intercostal artery. This requires immediate notification of the provider and likely emergent return to the OR. Concurrently: assess vital signs (BP, HR, SpO2), monitor for hemodynamic instability, prepare for potential blood transfusion, type and crossmatch if not already done, ensure large-bore IV access. The threshold for concern: >200 mL/hr for 2–4 hours, OR sudden spike to >300 mL/hr at any time.

250 mL/hr of bright red blood is never a 'document and wait' situation. This represents approximately 4 mL/min of active hemorrhage — a surgical emergency. Delayed response can result in hemorrhagic shock and death.
Increasing suction does not affect the rate of internal bleeding and would not be appropriate. Suction level adjustments are made for drainage efficiency, not in response to hemorrhage.
rat: Chest tube drainage assessment — normal vs. abnormal: Normal postoperative drainage: serosanguineous, 50–200 mL total in first 24 hours, decreasing over time. Concerning: >200 mL/hr sustained for 2+ hours = hemorrhage. Sudden bright red blood = active arterial bleeding — emergent. Clotting or sudden cessation of drainage in a patient who was bleeding heavily = clotted tube with ongoing hemorrhage — equally dangerous. Nursing actions for hemorrhage: notify provider immediately, vital signs, IV access and fluids, type and crossmatch, prepare for blood products, anticipate return to OR. Never clamp a chest tube without explicit order. Position: keep drainage system below chest level at all times. Document: color (serous, serosanguineous, sanguineous), amount, and consistency every hour in acute postoperative period.

stem: A patient receiving IV amiodarone for atrial fibrillation has a QTc interval of 520 ms on telemetry. Serum potassium is 3.1 mEq/L and magnesium is 1.4 mEq/L. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
opts: Notify the provider of the prolonged QTc and low electrolytes
Administer IV potassium replacement as ordered — hypokalemia potentiates QT prolongation
Administer IV magnesium replacement as ordered — hypomagnesemia contributes to QT prolongation and TdP risk
Continue amiodarone at the current rate — QTc prolongation is an expected and acceptable side effect
Monitor telemetry continuously for Torsades de Pointes
rat: QTc 520 ms with hypokalemia (K+ 3.1) and hypomagnesemia (Mg 1.4) in a patient on amiodarone creates a high-risk scenario for Torsades de Pointes. Three simultaneous QT-prolonging factors are present: amiodarone (class III antiarrhythmic — prolongs repolarization), hypokalemia (K+ <3.5 delays repolarization), and hypomagnesemia (Mg required for Na+/K+ ATPase function and membrane stability). Required actions: notify provider immediately (QTc >500 ms = critical threshold — provider must make decision about continuing amiodarone), replace potassium IV (target K+ >4.0 in patients at risk for dysrhythmias), replace magnesium IV (magnesium 2g IV even with borderline level — Mg deficiency prevents effective K+ replacement), continuous telemetry monitoring for Torsades. Continuing amiodarone at the current rate without provider notification is not appropriate — the QTc is critically prolonged and the decision to continue or hold requires clinical judgment by the prescriber.

stem: A patient involved in a motor vehicle accident arrives to the trauma bay with HR 138, BP 68/40 mmHg, distended neck veins, absent breath sounds on the left, and tracheal deviation to the right. The nurse recognizes this as obstructive shock from which cause, and what is the immediate priority intervention?
opts: Tension pneumothorax — prepare for immediate needle decompression of the left chest
Hemorrhagic shock — initiate massive transfusion protocol
Neurogenic shock — administer IV fluids and vasopressors for hypotension
optRationales: Cardiac tamponade presents with Beck's triad (muffled heart sounds, JVD, hypotension) and absent BREATH sounds would not be a primary feature. Tracheal deviation away from midline specifically indicates a mass effect — a tension pneumothorax is pushing mediastinal structures toward the opposite side. Tamponade does not cause tracheal deviation.

The classic presentation of tension pneumothorax: absent/decreased breath sounds on the affected side (left), tracheal deviation AWAY from the affected side (to the right — the tension is pushing everything over), JVD (impaired venous return as the mediastinum compresses the vena cava), and obstructive shock (hypotension + tachycardia). Mechanism: air enters the pleural space and cannot escape — progressive pressure collapses the ipsilateral lung and shifts the mediastinum, compressing the contralateral lung and kinking the great vessels. Immediate needle decompression — 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line, left side — is a life-saving emergency procedure. Do NOT wait for a chest X-ray.

Hemorrhagic shock presents with flat neck veins (low venous return), not JVD. Hemorrhagic shock does not cause tracheal deviation or unilateral absent breath sounds. The JVD plus absent breath sounds plus tracheal deviation is the classic triad of tension pneumothorax.
Neurogenic shock (from SCI) presents with bradycardia, hypotension, and warm skin — not tachycardia. There is no mechanism for tracheal deviation or absent breath sounds in neurogenic shock.
rat: Tension pneumothorax — obstructive shock: Air accumulates under pressure in the pleural space (penetrating trauma, rib fractures, barotrauma from MV). The trapped air progressively collapses the ipsilateral lung and shifts the mediastinum toward the contralateral side. Classic triad: absent breath sounds on affected side, tracheal deviation away from affected side, JVD (superior vena cava compression). Hemodynamic consequence: obstructive shock — the mediastinal shift kinks the SVC and IVC, preventing venous return and collapsing cardiac output. This is rapidly fatal without immediate intervention. Treatment: needle decompression IMMEDIATELY — 2nd ICS, midclavicular line (or 4th-5th ICS, anterior axillary line). A rush of air confirms diagnosis. Follow with chest tube insertion for definitive treatment. Do NOT wait for imaging if clinical signs are present — this is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate action.

stem: A patient in septic shock weighs 82 kg. The provider orders norepinephrine 0.08 mcg/kg/min. The pharmacy supplies norepinephrine 8 mg in 250 mL D5W. What is the correct infusion rate in mL/hr? Round to the nearest whole number.
optRationales: Correct. Step 1 — Concentration: 8 mg × 1000 = 8000 mcg ÷ 250 mL = 32 mcg/mL. Step 2 — Dose: 0.08 mcg/kg/min × 82 kg = 6.56 mcg/min. Step 3 — Per hour: 6.56 × 60 = 393.6 mcg/hr. Step 4 — Rate: 393.6 ÷ 32 = 12.3 mL/hr → 12 mL/hr. Always have a second nurse verify vasopressor pump settings before infusion.

15 mL/hr results from using an incorrect dose of 0.1 mcg/kg/min instead of 0.08 — a common error when rounding the ordered dose. Always transcribe the exact ordered dose and verify against the original order before calculating.

20 mL/hr results from a concentration error — using 24 mcg/mL instead of 32 mcg/mL, or calculating the dose with an incorrect weight. Double-check pharmacy label concentration before programming the pump.

24 mL/hr effectively doubles the correct rate — this would deliver approximately 0.16 mcg/kg/min, twice the ordered dose. Vasopressor overdose causes severe peripheral vasoconstriction, digital ischemia, and can precipitate hypertensive crisis. Critical care drug calculations require two-nurse verification.
rat: Norepinephrine drip rate calculation: (1) Concentration: 8 mg × 1000 mcg/mg = 8000 mcg ÷ 250 mL = 32 mcg/mL. (2) Dose: 0.08 mcg/kg/min × 82 kg = 6.56 mcg/min. (3) Per hour: 6.56 × 60 = 393.6 mcg/hr. (4) Rate: 393.6 ÷ 32 = 12.3 → 12 mL/hr. Framework for critical care drip calculations: convert all units first (mg→mcg), calculate dose using weight, convert to per-hour, divide by concentration. Two-nurse verification mandatory for all vasopressors. Administer via dedicated central line lumen when possible — peripheral extravasation causes tissue necrosis.

stem: A 94 kg patient with a pulmonary embolism requires heparin per weight-based protocol. The protocol orders: Bolus 80 units/kg IV, then initiate infusion at 18 units/kg/hr. The pharmacy provides heparin 25,000 units in 250 mL NS (100 units/mL). Calculate the initial infusion rate in mL/hr. Enter a whole number.
rat: Heparin weight-based protocol calculation: Bolus: 80 units/kg × 94 kg = 7,520 units IV bolus (given over 3–5 minutes). Infusion rate: 18 units/kg/hr × 94 kg = 1,692 units/hr. Concentration: 25,000 units ÷ 250 mL = 100 units/mL. mL/hr: 1,692 units/hr ÷ 100 units/mL = 16.92 mL/hr → rounds to 17 mL/hr. Nursing considerations: two-nurse verification required for heparin infusions. Monitor aPTT 6 hours after initiation and after any rate change — therapeutic range typically 60–100 seconds. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT): monitor platelet count every 2–3 days. Signs of bleeding: assess neuro status, urine/stool color, IV sites, back pain. Protamine sulfate is the reversal agent.

stem: A patient with DKA is on an IV regular insulin infusion per protocol. Current glucose is 340 mg/dL and the drip is running at 6 units/hr. The protocol states: 'If glucose does not decrease by at least 50–75 mg/dL per hour, increase infusion by 2 units/hr.' One hour ago glucose was 368 mg/dL. The nurse calculates the glucose dropped 28 mg/dL in the past hour. Which action is correct?
opts: Continue the current rate — a drop of 28 mg/dL is within the acceptable range
Decrease the insulin rate to 4 units/hr — glucose is falling and risks going too low
Increase the insulin infusion to 8 units/hr per protocol — the drop of 28 mg/dL is below the 50 mg/dL minimum target
Stop the insulin drip and recheck glucose in 2 hours — the patient needs a rest period
optRationales: A drop of 28 mg/dL per hour is below the minimum target of 50 mg/dL/hr. Continuing at the current rate when the protocol specifies escalation for inadequate response is not appropriate — it prolongs DKA resolution and increases complications.
Decreasing the rate is the opposite of what the protocol requires. The glucose is not falling fast enough — reducing insulin would worsen the inadequate response and prolong ketoacidosis.

The protocol criteria are met: the glucose dropped only 28 mg/dL in 1 hour, which is below the 50 mg/dL minimum target. Per protocol: increase by 2 units/hr. New rate: 6 + 2 = 8 units/hr. The nurse should also verify IV site patency and tubing (insulin adsorbs to PVC tubing — check if tubing was primed), then document the rate change and recheck glucose in 1 hour. If glucose still not dropping at 8 units/hr, reassess per protocol.

The insulin drip must NEVER be stopped in active DKA just because glucose response is slow — it must continue until the anion gap closes (pH >7.30, HCO3 >15, AG ≤12). Stopping the drip would allow unchecked ketogenesis to continue. The correct action is to increase the rate per protocol.
rat: DKA insulin drip protocol interpretation: Target glucose reduction = 50–75 mg/dL per hour. Actual drop = 368 − 340 = 28 mg/dL — below minimum target of 50. Protocol action: increase infusion by 2 units/hr → new rate = 8 units/hr. Before increasing: check IV site patency, verify tubing was primed with 20 mL of insulin solution (insulin adsorbs to PVC — underdelivery is a common cause of inadequate response), check for filters in the line (insulin does not pass through certain inline filters). Recheck glucose in 1 hour. When glucose reaches 250 mg/dL: add dextrose to IV fluids, reduce insulin to 0.05 units/kg/hr — do NOT stop drip. Continue until resolution criteria: pH >7.30, HCO3 >15, anion gap ≤12.
